title: How Much Does LASIK Cost? A 2026 Pricing Guide
summary: How much does LASIK cost? The average is about $2,246 per eye in 2026. See what affects the price, what's included, insurance, and financing options.
body_markdown:
If you've been wearing glasses or relying on contacts for years, you've probably wondered what it would take to stop. The short answer: in 2026, the average cost of LASIK eye surgery in the United States is about **$2,246 per eye** , according to[All About Vision](https://www.allaboutvision.com/treatments-and-surgery/vision-surgery/lasik/cost-of-lasik/) , or roughly **$4,500 for both eyes** . Quotes commonly range from about $1,500 to $5,000 per eye, depending on your location, the technology used, and the complexity of your prescription.


Keep in mind that national averages and quoted LASIK pricing almost always refer to a per-eye price. Ads showing a low base price often apply only to mild prescriptions with no astigmatism and basic laser technology, so the true cost of LASIK tends to be higher once you factor in the procedure details.


## Understanding LASIK Pricing: What Affects the Cost of LASIK?


LASIK surgery pricing is not standardized. Several factors determine what you'll pay, and the cost of LASIK at one center can differ dramatically from another even in the same city.


**Laser technology** is one of the biggest drivers. Surgeons price it in different ways: some charge one flat fee that covers every laser option, including bladeless LASIK, while others charge more for all-laser (bladeless) or custom wavefront-guided LASIK. The main options, from typically least to most expensive:


- **Traditional LASIK** , where a microkeratome blade creates the corneal flap
- **Bladeless (all-laser) LASIK** , where a femtosecond laser creates the flap
- **Custom wavefront-guided or topography-guided LASIK** , which uses more advanced technology to map your eye's unique imperfections and tailor the treatment


Other laser vision correction procedures, such as PRK (a surface treatment with no flap) and SMILE (a small-incision procedure), are priced in a similar range, with SMILE often at the higher end.


**Surgeon experience** significantly influences LASIK pricing. Highly experienced LASIK surgeons who perform a high volume of eye surgery often charge more, and their documented complication rates and expertise can justify the premium. A lower price may reflect less experience or older equipment.


**Location** affects LASIK pricing because rent, salaries, and local competition vary. Practices in large, high-cost cities tend to charge more than independent clinics in mid-sized cities. Higher prescriptions may also raise the cost of LASIK, since significant astigmatism, thin corneas, or complex corneal mapping often require custom treatment or an alternative vision correction procedure like PRK or SMILE.


Ask any potential LASIK provider for a written breakdown so you can compare quotes on equal terms.


## What's Included in the Cost of LASIK (and Hidden Fees to Watch For)


The cost of a LASIK procedure typically includes pre-operative exams, the surgery itself, and post-operative care visits, but it varies by provider. Ask exactly what's included in the price before you commit.


**Commonly bundled items:**


- Initial consultations and corneal mapping
- The LASIK procedure (surgeon fee, facility, laser use)
- Scheduled post-operative care visits
- At some clinics, one enhancement (touch-up) within a set period


**Common exclusions and hidden fees:**


- Prescription eye drops or artificial tears beyond the initial kit
- Follow-up visits beyond the bundled period
- Enhancements or retreatments after any warranty period
- Premium technology upcharges if you upgrade from a base-tier quote


LASIK providers use different pricing models. Some offer a flat fee per eye that covers the latest technology and all follow-ups. Others use tiered pricing where standard LASIK has one price and all-laser or wavefront-guided options carry a premium. Request a detailed written estimate that clarifies whether the quoted price is per eye or for both eyes, and exactly which services and timeframes are covered, so you know the overall cost. If you're paying yourself rather than through insurance, the No Surprises Act gives you the right to a[good faith estimate](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights) before scheduled care.


## LASIK vs. the Ongoing Cost of Glasses and Contact Lenses


Thinking of LASIK as an investment rather than a single bill changes the financial picture. Glasses and contact lenses are recurring costs: new frames and corrective lenses every year or two, a steady supply of contacts and solution, and regular eye exams.


To estimate your own break-even point, add up what you spend in a typical year on contacts, solution, and glasses, then divide your LASIK quote by that number. Keep in mind that many people still need one pair of reading glasses in their 40s and beyond, because LASIK can't correct presbyopia, the age-related loss of near vision, according to the[American Academy of Ophthalmology](https://www.aao.org/eye-health/treatments/lasik) .


Beyond the money, there are lifestyle factors worth weighing: waking up with clearer vision, not dealing with lost or broken glasses, and skipping daily contact lens care. These aren't financial gains, but for many patients they're a big part of the decision.


## Insurance Coverage and LASIK Financing Options


"Most medical insurance will not pay for refractive surgery," according to the[FDA](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/lasik/when-lasik-not-me) , because LASIK is generally considered elective, so insurance coverage is rare. That said, some vision insurance plans offer discounts or negotiated prices with certain LASIK surgeons or centers, so checking your plan is still worthwhile.


**LASIK financing** is widely available. Many LASIK centers offer in-house payment plans, and medical credit cards are another financing option. Promotional rates often depend on paying the balance in full within a set period, so review the interest rate and total repayment amount carefully before signing. Comparing financing options can make LASIK more affordable without adding much to the overall cost.


Tax-advantaged accounts are another way to plan for the cost.[IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) lists eye surgery to treat defective vision, such as laser eye surgery, as one of the medical expenses you can include. Whether you can use an HSA or FSA for it depends on your plan's rules, so check with your plan administrator. For 2026, HSA contribution limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage, and the health FSA limit is $3,400. Our guide to[HSAs and FSAs](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) explains how the two accounts compare.


## Is LASIK Eye Surgery Right for You? Candidacy, Safety, and Choosing a Surgeon


Not everyone is a good candidate for LASIK eye surgery. A comprehensive eye exam with a qualified refractive surgeon is the essential first step.


**Basic candidacy factors** , according to the[American Academy of Ophthalmology](https://www.aao.org/eye-health/treatments/lasik) and the[FDA](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/lasik/when-lasik-not-me) :


- Age 18 or older (ideally over 21, when vision is more likely to have stopped changing)
- A prescription that hasn't changed much in the past year
- Adequate corneal thickness and good overall eye health
- Nearsightedness, farsightedness, or astigmatism within treatable ranges
- No diseases or medications that affect healing


On outcomes, the American Academy of Ophthalmology reports that about 9 in 10 people who have LASIK end up with vision between 20/20 and 20/40 without glasses or contacts. Almost everyone has dry eyes and some changing vision at first, which usually fades within a month. Other possible side effects include glare, halos around lights, and reduced night vision. Serious complications are rare but possible, so assess the benefits and risks with your doctor.


When choosing among LASIK surgeons, ask how many procedures they've performed, their complication and enhancement rates, and which technology they use. A good LASIK provider will also discuss whether PRK or SMILE might be a better fit for your eyes.


Compare more than one provider, get every quote in writing, and don't let a limited-time promotion rush an informed decision about LASIK surgery.
